title: Iran Says Seven Tankers Hit in Hormuz, Warns US Bases Could Be Next
excerpt: The IRGC said four tankers were struck during oil transfers and three hit mines west of the strait. Washington called the claims fabricated, and neither account has been independently verified.
body:
• Iran's IRGC Navy said on Thursday, October 22, that four vessels carrying out ship-to-ship oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were hit simultaneously and caught fire, and three more vessels struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz — seven vessels in total.
  • The claims could not be independently verified: Iran named no ships, flags or casualties, and the UK Maritime Trade Operations monitor had not reported the incidents.
  • The IRGC warned that if the United States keeps helping tankers use routes Tehran calls unauthorised, the conflict will extend to US bases in the region.
  • Washington pushed back: President Donald Trump called the reports fabricated to push up oil prices before the US midterm elections, and US Central Command said the strait remains open with 95 percent of vessels getting through.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said on Thursday that seven vessels were hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz overnight, the largest single-day toll Tehran has claimed for the waterway since the United States and Israel began their war against Iran on February 28. Four vessels were struck while transferring oil in the northern Persian Gulf and caught fire, the IRGC said in a statement carried by Reuters. Three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait, caught fire and were stopped.

The IRGC said its forces had tracked the four tankers on Wednesday before striking them, and accused the US military of encouraging shipping companies to break navigation rules it has set for the strait. Iran claims control over Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the war broke out, and it regularly attacks ships that attempt to transit without its authorisation, Al Jazeera reported.

"The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region. This is a serious warning."

— Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, via Sepah News

Washington rejects the claims

The United States dismissed the Iranian account. President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform that Iran was "doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election" and was "making up fake hits, mines, and everything else," adding that more oil is moving through the strait now than before the conflict began. A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, called Iran's mine claims incorrect, said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines, and said the strait remains open, with 95 percent of vessels getting through. The spokesperson said the attacks showed Tehran's desperation under the US blockade.

The Associated Press reported that Iranian state television carried the claims, which it could not independently confirm, and that the report named no casualties. October has already seen the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March, in the war's opening weeks, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a British military monitor. UKMTO did not report the latest incidents, but it has noted growing reluctance among some shipping operators to report attacks at all.

Context: a war that never fully stopped

The Hormuz claims land days before a close election in Israel on October 27, in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and ahead of next month's US midterm elections, where war-linked fuel prices have angered voters. The United States is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, joining the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades, AP reported. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that Tehran remains open to diplomacy but is ready to defend itself. Iran still promotes a proposal to end the war and fully reopen the strait within a week if the United States meets several conditions, including ending its blockade of Iranian ports. Trump rejected that seven-day proposal in late September, though both sides acknowledge indirect discussions have continued.

Impact and what is next

Hormuz is Iran's central point of leverage over Washington: the threat to shipping through the strait is what converts a regional war into a global oil-price event. A return to all-out fighting would complicate worldwide deliveries of oil, natural gas and products such as fertiliser, and likely bring another price spike. For India, which imports the bulk of its crude, sustained disruption in the Gulf feeds directly into fuel costs at home and the remittance-linked economies of the Gulf states, where millions of Indian workers live. Mediators are still trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks. Until they succeed, each claimed attack raises the question of whether the shipping war stays a pressure tactic or triggers wider strikes, potentially including US bases.
